item.title: Ousted Paraguayan president placed under house arrest after bank collapse
item.description: Ousted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay -- Ousted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust and influence peddling, among other charges, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country’s 6 million people out of their savings. All 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second Paraguayan president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner’s 35-year dictatorship in 1989. As the verdict came down, ending what had been seen as one of South America’s most stable presidencies, a roar rose from the crowds packed into the plaza outside Congress. Depositors, retirees and students in national soccer jerseys waved Paraguayan flags, sang and hugged, chanting “Dictatorship never again!” Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country’s worst political crisis in more than a decade. An ousted president, under house arrest Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asuncion until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. Peña has denied wrongdoing. Police ringed the house Friday night as crowds gathered outside, waving flags and vowing to keep vigil until morning to make sure he didn’t escape. Prosecutors also ordered the arrest of Carlos Carvallo, who ran the finance company that became Ueno until Peña named him central bank chief in 2023. It was not immediately clear whether Carvallo had been taken into custody. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term, which ends in August 2028. “The Paraguay we receive today has urgent needs,” said Alliana, who is also under investigation in connection with the bank and inherits a government under pressure to return depositors’ money and punish those responsible. In a farewell message before the verdict, Peña said that he did not want his “presence to be a cause of greater division or instability.” “I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today.” Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day. As senators deliberated Friday, crowds of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno’s failure marched through downtown Asuncion chanting, “Santi Peña to Tacumbu!” -- a reference to the capital’s main prison, where Ueno’s founder and former CEO, Miguel Vazquez, is now being held. “This was an enormous betrayal of trust,” said Yinal Lopez, a worker at the state electricity company, whose employee pension fund also had money at Ueno. “The president has made a mockery of the people. Frozen accounts, rising anger When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can’t reach their money. The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says US$21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay’s bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guarani has slid against the dollar. Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaranies (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97 per cent of Ueno’s customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe. In a separate case against Ueno’s executives, prosecutors have charged 27 people, including Vazquez, with crimes such as breach of trust and attempted fraud.A judge has ordered six former directors, Vazquez among them, held in pretrial detention, and two others confined to their homes with electronic monitors. Authorities have seized luxury cars, a yacht and two small planes linked to Vazquez. A bank built on public money Ueno rose from obscurity to become one of Paraguay’s largest banks by deposits in just a few years, with more than $800 million in public money turbocharging its expansion. It signed up more than two-thirds of the country’s adults, its splashy logo appearing everywhere from the national soccer stadium to street vendors’ bank cards. The impeachment charges cite Peña’s stake in Ueno’s holding company, which he divested under pressure last year, and his appointment of Carvallo to run the central bank that regulated it. Lawmakers also accuse him of letting the state pension fund deposit $355 million at the bank, beyond legal limits. Analysts say those high-level connections helped shield Ueno from regulatory scrutiny even as concerns about its finances grew. “Under Peña, the central bank began to lose credibility, lose neutrality and then relax all its control mechanisms to favor the business group that had Ueno Bank as one of its pillars,” said Jose Tomas Sanchez, a political theory professor at the National University of Asuncion. Peña defended the bank until mere weeks before it failed, telling reporters last month that a regulatory inquiry into Ueno didn’t mean it would close and accusing the media of frightening people. A bank collapse becomes a political reckoning Peña’s fall, from feted Washington ally meeting with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in late October to prisoner in his own home, came at dizzying speed. Ueno was seized before dawn Tuesday. By Thursday afternoon, Peña had offered to resign as his conservative Colorado party turned on him, led by former President Horacio Cartes, the party chief and Peña’s longtime mentor. By Friday, he was under arrest, with impeachment denying him the immunity he would have enjoyed if the Senate had accepted his resignation. Peña, a former International Monetary Fund economist, owed his rise to Cartes, a tobacco magnate who made him finance minister and twice backed him for president. Once in office, though, Peña sought to escape Cartes’ shadow by quietly building his own power base, analysts say. Ueno, flush with public funds, became its linchpin. “It’s like a Shakespearean drama. He tried to displace his mentor, his political patron,” said Miguel Carter, director of DEMOS, a Paraguayan research center. “But he did so on very fragile grounds.” Cartes struck back. In September, senators loyal to him began publicly questioning the central bank about Ueno’s risky lending to related companies. When Ueno collapsed this week, so did Peña’s leverage, and Cartes, once sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury over alleged corruption, publicly called for the ouster of his erstwhile protege. “Cartes put the nail in the coffin,” said Andrew Nickson, a Paraguay expert at the University of Birmingham. “Peña had no political base to rely on, and he was left high and dry.” ___ Isabel Debre, Nayara Batschke and Emilio Sanabria, The Associated Press DeBre reported from Salto, Uruguay, and Batschke from Montevideo, Uruguay.

item.title: Investor Outlook: Côté gold mine stake buyout aims to lower costs
item.description: IAMGOLD CEO Renaud Adams discusses third-quarter earnings, gold production and plans to buy out a financial stake in the Côté mine.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: IAMGOLD’s latest quarterly results put its Canadian and West African gold operations in focus. Operational performance and capital allocation frame the discussion heading into year-end. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Renaud Adams, president and CEO at IAMGOLD, about the results and the company’s priorities. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: LINDSAY: IAMGOLD reported its third-quarter revenue and profit, beating analyst estimates in its third quarter. The company reaffirmed its annual production guidance and announced plans to buy out a financial interest in its Côté mine. Let’s get more now from Renaud Adams, president and CEO at IAMGOLD. It’s great to have you join us this morning. Thanks for taking the time. RENAUD: No, thank you. It’s great. It’s a great time at IAMGOLD. So, very pleased to be here, too. LINDSAY: Well, I mean, you are generating significant cash flow at current gold prices. So we’ll start there because, like, how much of that profitability would remain if gold prices pulled back even to, like, $3,500? RENAUD: Well, we’re in a pretty good, pretty good position. You know, like, we’ve completed the construction of our main asset, Côté Gold. We’ve ramped it up. We have, we do have, of course, organic growth capital over the next few years. But they’re more optimizations in nature. So we’re very, very well equipped, you know, to, to continue to generate significant free cash flow should the gold price pull back a bit. We’ve made our plan at $4,000, and it’s been, it’s been a very good, a very good free cash flow generation so far this year. And, but no, I think we’re extremely well equipped now with Côté fully ramped up, achieving nameplate, and looking forward to continuing to optimize the asset, which will shave — and on the same basis of continuing to protect ourselves and continue generating good cash flow. So, you’ve seen that we’ve announced a repurchase of — yeah. LINDSAY: I want to talk about all of that, but I just want to start with the Côté mine because September was your best throughput month ever. Is that a new normal? Was that a one-off? What was going on there? RENAUD: Well, the asset and the mine were designed, you know, for 36,000 tonnes a day. So, in the very early days, we were extremely successful in achieving the first goal, the nameplate, the nameplate. But there was technically something missing, and we installed new secondary crushing, and that was done at the end of Q2. So Q3 2026 was really our first quarter where we were operating without any additional external contracting, contracting crushing, and we have achieved, we have achieved above the nameplate. So I think now the asset is well ramped up. It’s a matter more of optimization and reducing unit costs down the road. But we’re achieving now the nameplate, and we’re focusing on our first full quarter in Q4 achieving nameplate without any additional external contracting. LINDSAY: I want to talk also about what you announced on your earnings call this morning. You mentioned it: the plan to buy out Franco-Nevada’s 7.5 per cent financial stake in the Côté gold mine. Why was now the right time to do that, do you think? RENAUD: Well, this is the right time because of the gold price mostly, and because of extensions of our mine life. So, up to, up to now, the asset was built on the basis of about 10 million ounces of resources and seven million ounces of reserves, and this quarter we’ll be, we’ll be announcing the results of our, of our new, updated 43-101 for Côté Gold, which would highlight a significant increase in reserves and an extension of the mine life. Combined with that, at the time that Franco acquired the NPI, it was at a much lower gold price. So when you combine an extension of reserves, mine life and a higher gold price, it becomes a no-brainer for us to jump on this opportunity that we had secured back in, back in 2025, and we feel very strongly about it. And our partner Sumitomo decided not to participate, which increased even further the benefit for us. We have excess cash flow. We have returned significant cash to our shareholders through the share buyback. We’re looking to potentially initiate a dividend early this year, and nonetheless, we continue to have excess cash flow. So we make sure that all our assets are very well equipped to unlock the maximum value down the road, and we thought that, as, as excess cash, it was the best place to position it and just buy back more of our main asset in Canada. LINDSAY: Sumitomo’s decision not to participate, like, how does that affect your relationship with your joint-venture partner going forward? Does it at all? RENAUD: Oh, absolutely, absolutely no issues. We have a very great partner. We’ve done good and continue to do good things. Everyone, every company has its priorities and cash and capital allocations. What defines us really is the significant free cash flow generation and excess cash, which is not necessarily the case for all industries. But it doesn’t impact it at all, and we remain in a very strong relationship. But we all have different capital allocation priorities. That’s the way we look at it. LINDSAY: You’ve also reaffirmed guidance of 720,000 to 820,000 ounces for the year. Which operations out of the main three are contributing the most into the fourth quarter, do you think, of your mines? RENAUD: Well, they’re all contributing very strongly. Côté Gold has unfortunately had a little bit of an operational issue in the first quarter, which has been fixed since then. We had a very good second, third, and the fourth quarter will be by far our strongest quarter. But our two other mines, the second mine in Burkina and Westwood in Quebec, have been performing extremely well, with Westwood trending to the top end of its guidance. So I would say it’s a, it’s a combined effort, but for Q4, we’re expecting Côté to lead the charge with the strongest production. LINDSAY: But Côté costs did come in above your own guidance range, right? Like, how much of that is a one-time thing versus something that, that really carries into next year? RENAUD: Well, there’s been a bit of inflation, of course, with the fuel situation. There’s been a little bit of adjustment there on the power as well, a bit of pressure sometimes on the, on, on the labour. But what is ultimately the biggest impact is the gold price. So it goes both ways. It goes on the free cash flow generation, of course, that is significantly higher, but it also impacts, you know, the cost of royalties across our assets. We’re averaging about $370 an ounce this year. So, of course, if you reduce the gold price, it would reduce free cash flow, but it would also reduce significantly. So, along the same topic of reducing costs, so this is another big aspect of buying back the NPI, is to reduce significantly this, this burden on royalties. And so buying back this, this 50 per cent from Franco effectively reduces by $150 or so, starting in 2027, the cost at Côté Gold. LINDSAY: OK, we’ve got to leave it there. We are out of time. Renaud Adams, president and CEO at IAMGOLD. Appreciate you joining us. Thank you. RENAUD: Thank you so much. Have a great day. LINDSAY: You too. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Nov. 6, 2026 interview with Renaud Adams are published with the assistance of AI. Original research, interview questions and added context was created by BNN Bloomberg journalists. item.title: Economists concerned after labour market sheds jobs for third month in a row
item.description: Some economists are getting worried that a string of job losses in recent months is revealing cracks in the labour market.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Some economists are getting worried that a string of job losses in recent months is revealing cracks in the labour market. Statistics Canada said Friday that the unemployment rate rose two tenths of a point to 6.7 per cent in October. The labour market shed 4,700 jobs last month, the agency said, and more people were also looking for work. October’s modest decline followed a cumulative loss of 110,000 jobs across September and August. A Reuters poll of economists had expected the economy would bounce back with a gain of 13,600 jobs in October. “For anyone hoping that October would bring a recovery in the Canadian job market after back-to-back negative surprises, today’s release is a disappointment,” said Sneha Puri, economist with jobs search site Indeed, in a media statement. Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions last month, marking the first decline in the segment since February. Employment in the public sector, meanwhile, was up 50,000 positions. StatCan noted that, on a year-over-year basis, private sector jobs are still up while the public sector is down. Employment in the wholesale and retail trade industry has trended down over the past year and the sector led losses in October, shedding 29,000 roles. Transportation and warehousing and food and accommodation also posted losses last month, offset by some gains in construction and education. CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham said in an interview that he had expected more of a lift in the October labour market from one-time factors like the Alberta referendum. While he had been anticipating the jobless rate would tick up in the fourth quarter in the face of tariff-related headwinds, Friday’s employment figures suggest there’s more underlying softness in the jobs market. “It does look as if we’re seeing some weakness in the labour market outside of those trade-sensitive areas. So that’s a concern for us right now,” Grantham said. That could dampen expectations for a rebound in job growth in 2027, he added. The unemployment rate for young workers aged 15 to 24 jumped to 13.7 per cent in October, up 0.7 percentage points from September, as employment edged down and more youth looked for work. Young workers have faced a generally tough labour market in recent years but there had been little change in the jobless rate for the age group over the summer. StatCan said the unemployment rate was higher for students compared with youth not attending school. The agency said the layoff rate – the proportion of people employed in September who were laid off by October – was “virtually unchanged” compared with a year earlier at 0.7 per cent. Average hourly wages rose 2.2 per cent annually in October, edging down from 2.3 per cent in September. Puri said Indeed’s Canadian job postings ticked up at the end of last month, which could be an indication of future hiring. If Canada can gain clarity on U.S. trade policy in the wake of the midterm elections this week, she said that could give employers the confidence to hire again. “If this optimism isn’t then translated into a strong jobs report in the months ahead, the surprising weakness in headline employment will start to look less temporary and more like the beginning of a renewed cooling in the labour market,” Puri warned. The October job figures come a little over a week after the Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike in more than three years, raising its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent. Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the uptick in the unemployment rate and muted wage growth should tell the Bank of Canada that there’s still slack in the job market right now. The October jobs data should therefore push back on calls for much more tightening of monetary policy, he argued. “Ultimately, this adds to our conviction that the bank will hike rates no more than twice more as a precaution against upside inflation risks, before calling it a day,” Ryan said. Financial market odds of another quarter-point hike at the Bank of Canada’s final rate decision of the year on Dec. 9 stood at 35 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. Bank of Canada officials made clear after the October rate hike that their focus is on getting ahead of inflationary pressures spreading from the global energy shock, Grantham noted. Soft labour market data and recent declines in the benchmark price of oil take pressure of the central bank to deliver another rate hike next month, he said. “We have a lot of days for oil prices to do something volatile between now and December. But if those two forces stay in effect, we do forecast that they will hold interest rates at the December meeting,” Grantham said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026. By Craig Lord
